h: פָּרָשַׁת הַחֹדֶשׁ, מַאֲמָר ה׳ Parshas HaChodesh — Maamar Hei

p: and so too in the Yerushalmi
(רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ג ז, ב)
it is handed over to you.
It is like a king who had a clock;
he handed over his clock to him.
Like a king who had watchmen;
he handed over the watch to him.
Like a king who had a ring;
when his son grew up, he handed it to him.
Like a king who had treasuries;
לְמֶלֶךְ שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ כְּלֵי אוּמָּנוּת כּוּלֵּי
Like a king who had craftsman's tools" etc.
כֵּיוָן שֶׁעָמַד בְּנוֹ מָסַר לוֹ כּוּלֵּי
when his son grew up, he handed it to him" etc.
We need to understand the meaning of these parables.
For a clock, which is an instrument of hours,
it makes sense that he used it as a parable
for the sanctification of the month, which concerns time;
but what is the point of the watch,
and craftsman's tools, and a case of remedies,
But the matter is as we said (in the previous maamar)
בְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה
on "and a desire fulfilled is a tree of life":
that it is the words of Torah
in the utterance "This month shall be for you."
And it says He handed them the watch,
in the manner of what we say
(the piyut Ki Anu Amecha for Yom Kippur):
"We are Your vineyard and You are our Keeper" —
for Hashem Yisbarach is the Guardian of Yisrael;
"For He will hide me in His shelter" etc.,
that, as it were, Hashem Yisbarach
And this He handed over to Yisrael,
which is called a "shelter of peace"
"so the Holy One, blessed be He, leaps
מִבֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת זוֹ לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת זוֹ
from this shul to that shul,
וּמִבֵּית הַמִּדְרָשׁ זֶה לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ זֶה כּוּלֵּי
and from this beis midrash to that beis midrash" etc.;
"And I will be for them a small sanctuary,"
and batei midrash in Bavel" etc.,
"this is the house of our Rebbe in Bavel."
And "Hashem loves the gates of Zion" —
יוֹתֵר מִבָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת וּבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת כּוּלֵּי
more than the shuls and batei midrash etc.:
from there is the root of Torah she'b'al peh,
"For from Zion will Torah go forth" etc.;
and there is the Chamber of Hewn Stone,
from which Torah goes forth to all Yisrael
And this is what it says: "This month shall be for you" —
the renewal of Torah she'b'al peh
and this is the Beis HaMikdash
and the four amos of halachah,
which are called a "shelter of peace";
and this is what they said in the parable,
that he handed his son the watch.
And afterward it gives the parable
"Like a king who had a ring" etc. —
it is along the lines of what they said
"Like a king for whom they made a ring;
what was it lacking? A seal.
So too the world was lacking Shabbos";
The creation of heaven and earth is the ring,
meaning that it should remain so,
in the manner of what it says (Esther 8:8),
"And what is sealed with the king's ring
וְחוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֱמֶת
And the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, is truth,
Alef at the beginning of the letters,
mem in the middle, tav at the end";
עַל שֵׁם אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן וַאֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן.
after "I am first and I am last."
which signifies "was, is and will be";
and this is Shabbos, which is the seal.
As we say on Shabbos (in the Minchah prayer),
"You are One and Your Name is One" —
all the holiness of Havayah up to Atika,
for the Name Havayah contains the nine middos
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג רנח, א)
and the upper tip of the Yud
and "The lip of truth shall be established forever,"
and "what is sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked."
And this He handed to Yisrael,
for they then became a chariot
Keser Elyon is the Crown of Malchus.
And afterward it says the parable
"Like a king who had treasuries" etc.:
that is, "the fear of Hashem is His treasure,"
for the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing
but a treasury of fear of Heaven
אִם יֵשׁ לְךָ יִרְאַת חֵטְא כּוּלֵּי
"if you have fear of sin" etc. —
And "keys" refers to what they said (Shabbos 31b):
which are Torah and fear of Heaven.
פֶּה תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה קָרִינָן לָהּ
"the mouth: we call it Torah she'b'al peh"
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק א ה, ב)
and the Name corresponding to this attribute
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג יא, ב)
And this is why he likened
what it says, "This month shall be for you" —
which is the attribute of Malchus,
the aspect of the moon that receives from the sun —
to treasuries he handed over to his son,
according to the version of the Yerushalmi,
or to keys he handed over to his son,
as they said in the Pesikta.
And afterward it says the parable
"Like a king who had craftsman's tools,"
and in the Yerushalmi, "Like a carpenter
of the Holy One, blessed be He";
for the creation of the world was through the Torah;
"and in His goodness He renews each day
שֶׁמְּחַדֵּשׁ בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה בְּכָל יוֹם
that He innovates in the heavenly court every day
and this renewal of halachos He handed to Yisrael,
on account of which they are called "builders,"
for they are engaged in the building of the world
And this is why he likened it to craftsman's tools
that he handed over to his son,
for they are called "your builders," as mentioned above.
And afterward it says the parable
וְהַיְינוּ גַּם כֵּן עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
this too refers to words of Torah,
"It shall be healing to your navel" etc.,
for with words of Torah everything can be healed,
and I created Torah as its antidote";
and this helps to repair the root of the corruption.
And here he likened Hashem Yisbarach to a physician,
"He heals the wound of His blow" —
"He will heal the wound of the world's blow"
that is, through Torah she'b'al peh,
drag him to the beis midrash";
וּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ הוּא מְקוֹם חִידּוּשׁ הֲלָכוֹת
and the beis midrash is the place where halachos are renewed,
And this He handed over to Yisrael,
as it is written, "This month shall be for you,"
namely the flow of influence in Torah she'b'al peh;
and this is what they said in the parable,
that he handed him a case of remedies.
וְשַׁבָּת אִיתָא (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א מז, ב)
And regarding Shabbos it is stated (Zohar I 47b):
פֶּה תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה קָרִינָן לָהּ
"the mouth: we call it Torah she'b'al peh";
and so we read Parshas HaChodesh

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 15 — “‘This month shall be for you’—it is entrusted to you. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: This is like a king who had a clock; when his son came of age, he handed him his clock. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said: Like a king who had a guard-post; when his son came of age, he handed him the guard-post. Rabbi Acha said: Like a king who had a ring; when his son came of age, he handed him his ring. Rabbi Yitzchak said: Like a king who had treasuries, with a key for each; when his son came of age, he handed him the keys. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said: Like a king who had tools of his craft; when his son came of age, he handed him his tools. The Sages said: Like a physician who had a case of medicines; when his son came of age, he handed him his case.” The parallel passage in Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 1:3 gives a carpenter with his tools, and says that the treasuries themselves were handed over. Rav Tzadok expressly distinguishes these readings in developing the parables. The Pesikta’s traditional internal §18 is retained as the manuscript’s locator; the complete digital chapter 15 supplies the checked wording.

paragraphs.text: Yom Kippur Machzor, Ki Anu Amecha — “For we are Your people and You are our God. We are Your children and You are our Father. We are Your servants and You are our Master. We are Your assembly and You are our portion. We are Your inheritance and You are our lot. We are Your flock and You are our Shepherd. We are Your vineyard and You are our Keeper. We are Your handiwork and You are our Maker. We are Your beloved and You are our Beloved.” The vineyard and its keeper are one of the poem’s paired images of Israel and God. Rav Tzadok applies this particular image to God’s guarding Israel.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 15 — “‘My beloved resembles a deer.’ Rabbi Yitzchak said: Just as a deer leaps and springs from tree to tree, from shelter to shelter, and from fence to fence, so the Holy One, blessed be He, leaps from this synagogue to that synagogue, and from this study hall to that study hall. For what purpose? To bless Israel. Through what merit? Through the merit of his sitting at the oaks of Mamre, as it is written, ‘Hashem appeared to him at the oaks ... while he was sitting at the entrance of the tent.’” The Midrash continues with God’s assurance to Avraham that, while his descendants sit in synagogues and study halls, His glory will stand among them. This identifies the protection of the parable with an active divine presence in communal Torah and prayer; §9 is the manuscript’s internal division.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Beha'aloscha 3 — “Once the Mishkan was set up, where the Shechinah rests, which is Malchus, called Torah she'b'al peh… the essence of the Oral Torah was in the Lishkas HaGazis in the Mikdash.” This explains why the Mikdash is the root of the Oral Torah. The place of the Shechinah is Malchus, the “mouth,” and so the Oral Torah goes forth from there.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 10:9 — “Geniva said: This is like a king for whom they made a bridal chamber; they fashioned and decorated it. What was it lacking? A bride to enter it. So what was the world lacking? Shabbos. The Sages said: This is like a king for whom they made a ring. What was it lacking? A seal. So what was the world lacking? Shabbos.” The two parables express completion through the arrival of Shabbos. Rav Tzadok develops the second specifically as the seal that gives creation its enduring character.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 81:2 — “What is the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He? Our teacher said in the name of Rabbi Reuven: Truth. What is truth? Reish Lakish said: Alef is at the beginning of the letters, mem in the middle, and tav at the end, corresponding to ‘I am first and I am last.’” The complete span of the alphabet grounds Rav Tzadok’s reading of truth as embracing beginning, present continuity, and end.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Agra DeKallah (R' Tzvi Elimelech of Dinov), Bereishis Rabbah 10 — “The ring is the natural order, conducted by the Name Elokim, which equals ‘hateva’; to those who keep Shabbos is given the conduct above nature, through the Name Havayah.” From another school this matches Rav Tzadok’s reading. The ring is creation. The seal of Shabbos is the Name Havayah set upon it.

paragraphs.text: Siddur Ashkenaz, Shabbos Minchah, middle blessing — “You are One, and Your name is One; and who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth? Splendor and greatness, and a crown of salvation—a day of rest and holiness You have given Your people. Avraham rejoices, Yitzchak sings, and Yaakov and his sons rest upon it: a rest of love and generosity, a rest of truth and faith, a rest of peace, tranquility, quiet and security; a complete rest that You desire. May Your children recognize and know that their rest comes from You, and through their rest sanctify Your name.” The prayer connects divine unity, Israel’s unity, the patriarchs and the sanctity of rest. Rav Tzadok invokes its opening in explaining Shabbos as the seal.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 258a, Pinchas (Raaya Mehemna) — “The tefillin of the Master of the world are Keser. And what is the Keser of the Master of the world? Havayah: Yud is Chochmah, Hei is Binah, Vav is Tiferes, which comprises six sefiros, and Hei is Malchus.” The four letters thus include the nine attributes from Chochmah to Malchus, and Keser is the crown above them. Rav Tzadok then refers the tip of the Yud to Keser, from Zohar III 65b.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 30:14 — “If a person learns Midrash, halachos, and aggados, but has no fear of sin, he has nothing. This is like a person who told his friend: ‘I have a thousand measures of grain, a thousand of oil, and a thousand of wine.’ His friend said: ‘Do you have storehouses in which to place them? If you do, they are all yours; otherwise you have nothing.’ So, if a person has fear of sin, everything is his; otherwise he has nothing.” The Midrash cites “Fear of Hashem is His treasury.” Its storehouses are the capacity to retain and make effective the accumulated learning, which explains the parable of handing over treasuries.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 2 — on “I have a good gift in My treasure-house, and Shabbos is its name” (Shabbos 10b): “this is fear, as it says: Hashem has in His treasure-house only a treasury of fear of Heaven.” Rav Tzadok there links the treasury, fear and Shabbos. This is why the treasury entrusted to Yisrael in Nisan is read on Shabbos.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 31a–b — “A person who possesses Torah but does not possess fear of Heaven resembles a treasurer to whom the inner keys were entrusted, but the outer keys were not entrusted. Through what can he enter? Rabbi Yannai proclaimed: Woe to one who has no courtyard, yet makes a gate for the courtyard!” The opening words of Rabbah bar Rav Huna’s statement begin at the end of 31a and continue on 31b. Torah and reverence function together; the keys of the inner chambers are ineffective without access through the outer entrance.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 5b, Introduction — “Another Shabbos remained unmentioned and was ashamed. She said before Him: ‘Master of the world, from the day You made me I have been called Shabbos, yet there is no day without night.’ He said to her: ‘My daughter, you are Shabbos and I call you Shabbos, but I now crown you with a higher crown.’ He issued a proclamation: ‘My Sanctuary you shall fear.’ This is the Shabbos of Shabbos eve, which is fear, and fear rests within her.” The passage’s 5b marker precedes this teaching, and 6a follows it. The sanctity of Shabbos night is expressly joined to reverence, explaining its relation to the guarding aspect of Malchus.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 11b, Vayikra — “The ninth is Shaddai, for He said to the world, ‘Enough’; enough is sufficiency, and sufficiency comes to the world only from the tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world. The tenth is Adonai, for the law of kingship is assuredly law. This is to wage the King’s battles in the world; this is the lower Gevurah, and this is righteousness.” This is the second enumeration in the chapter; the preceding passage carries 11b. The final name belongs to the royal aspect, explaining Rav Tzadok’s invocation of “If I am a master, where is My fear?” in Malachi 1:6.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 49:2 — “Rabbi Berechyah, Rabbi Chiya, and the Sages there said in the name of Rabbi Yehudah: There is no day on which the Holy One, blessed be He, does not renew a halachah in the heavenly court. What is its basis? ‘Listen carefully to the thunder of His voice, and the utterance that goes out from His mouth.’ Utterance here means only Torah, as it is said: ‘You shall meditate upon it day and night.’ Even those halachos Avraham knew.” The daily renewal of Torah gives content to the continuing use of the craftsman’s tools, rather than limiting the image to creation in the past.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 114a — “Who are the builders? Rabbi Yochanan said: These are Torah scholars, who occupy themselves with building the world throughout all their days.” In its immediate discussion, the Gemara asks which people are designated by the Mishnah’s term “builders.” Rav Tzadok develops the answer as the formative power of their ongoing halachic work.

paragraphs.text: Proverbs 4:22 — “For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.” The antecedent is the instruction to attend to the speaker’s words and preserve them within the heart. Mishlei 3:8 similarly promises, “It will be healing to your navel and refreshment to your bones.” The two verses underlie the medicine-case parable.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 10:4 — “Before the first man sinned, the heavenly bodies traveled by a short course and swiftly. Once he sinned, He made them go round by a long course and slowly. ... But in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will heal that wound, as it is said: ‘He will heal the injury of its wound’—He will heal the injury of the world’s wound.” Yeshayahu 30:26 speaks of the day God binds His people’s injury and heals its wound. The Midrash places the wound and its future healing within the cosmic consequence of Adam’s sin.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 30b — “The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: If this repulsive one encounters you, draw him to the study hall. If he is stone, he will melt; if he is iron, he will shatter. If he is stone, he will melt, as it is said: ‘All who thirst, go to water,’ and ‘Water wears away stones.’ If he is iron, he will shatter, as it is said: ‘Are not My words like fire, declares Hashem, and like a hammer that shatters rock?’” This passage specifies the study hall as the place of Torah’s action against the inclination. Rav Tzadok emphasizes its character as the place where new halachic understanding emerges.
